reply.conflict: The paragraph's claim that "F ≤ 1 - 1/k for k claim classes" (and the derived numeric ceiling 0.8889 for k=9).

reply.conflict: The paragraph's claim: "The stated ceiling is F ≤ 1 - 1/k, where k is the number of claim classes."

Plugging in the distribution with k = N (each class has n_c = 1) gives ∑_c n_c(n_c - 1) = 0 and therefore F = 1, which is greater than 1 - 1/k = 1 - 1/N. Thus the paper's own formula for F permits values exceeding 1 - 1/k, contradicting the asserted universal bound.
reply.explanation: The paragraph asserts a universal upper bound F ≤ 1 - 1/k, but the paper's own definition of F (Equation 2) shows that F can exceed 1 - 1/k for some class-count distributions (e.g., each class having one specification), so the 'ceiling' statement is not generally valid within the paper's formalism.

No internal contradictions were found.

The caption describes the three probe conditions (source-trained on full representations and on top-100 PCs, and target-trained on top-100 source PCs with 5-fold CV), which matches the experimental setup in Section 3 and the results described in Section 4.1 (the AUROC values reported there correspond to these conditions). There is no contradiction elsewhere in the paper.

The AUROC numbers given (Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606) are used consistently elsewhere in the paper (e.g., Section 4.5 and Section 5) and align with the other reported baseline and target-trained figures, so no internal conflict is found.

Insider Trading Confirm: greedy {PC71,PC53,PC28,PC86,PC32,PC81,PC77} vs target {PC4,PC1,PC8,PC53,PC30,PC7,PC13,PC18,PC5,PC20,PC26,PC49,PC28,PC31,PC97} → intersection {PC53,PC28} size 2, union size 20 → Jaccard = 2/20 = 0.10. reply.explanation: The paper uses a and b inconsistently: the joint definition designates a as hidden biases and b as visible biases, but the conditional P(h_j=1|...) incorrectly uses b_j where a_j should appear (and P(v_i=1|h) conversely uses a_i), so the bias symbols are swapped/inconsistent.

reply.conflict: The paragraph gives P(v_i = 1 | h) = σ(a_i + Σ_j W_{ij} h_j), i.e. it uses a_i as the visible-unit bias.
reply.evidence: Earlier in Section 8.1 the paper defines the joint distribution as P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), which makes a the hidden-unit bias vector and b the visible-unit bias vector. Given that definition, the conditional should be P(v_i=1|h)=σ(b_i + Σ_j W_{ij} h_j), so the paragraph's formula conflicts with the earlier notation.
reply.explanation: The paragraph's conditional uses 'a' for the visible bias while the joint distribution earlier in the section assigns 'b' as the visible bias (and 'a' as the hidden bias); thus the bias symbols are inconsistent between equations.

The statement exactly matches the formal model in Section 8.1: P(h,v|r;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) with g(h_j,r_j) forcing h_j=0 when r_j=0, so conditioned on r the distribution is an RBM over the retained hidden subset. Thus viewing the Dropout RBM as a mixture (over r) of RBMs with shared weights is consistent with the paper's definitions and equations.

reply.conflict: "Smaller p requires big n which slows down the training and leads to underfitting."

reply.explanation: The paragraph implies that making p smaller (and thus increasing n) leads to underfitting. Elsewhere the paper shows the opposite: if n is scaled up (keeping pn constant) then small p can improve generalization (reduce error). The paragraph conflates the fixed-n and scaled-n cases and thus makes a claim inconsistent with the experiments and guidance given in Appendix A.1 and Section 7.3.

reply.conflict: The paragraph asserts that C4Y is "representing negative KL divergence between target and predicted distributions, with higher values preferred."

reply.explanation: The appendix definition differs from (is not equal to) negative KL between target and predicted distributions: C4Y = -KL(p||q) + KL(p||\bar p), so it is not simply negative KL as claimed.

reply.evidence:
Section 9.1 immediately provides the analytic derivation: the marginalized objective reduces to
||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||\Gamma w||^2 with \Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With \widetilde w = p w this becomes ||y - X \widetilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||\Gamma \widetilde w||^2. Thus the penalty is weighted by the feature column norms (proportional to standard deviation) and the effective regularization constant is (1-p)/p, which is small for p near 1 and larger for smaller p.
reply.explanation: The paragraph's informal claims are a direct summary of the explicit formulas in Section 9.1: the penalty matrix scales weights by feature-scale and the regularization strength behaves as (1-p)/p, decreasing near complete retention and increasing with more removal.

The paragraph's notation and assumptions (X ∈ ℝ^{N×D}, w ∈ ℝ^D, elementwise Bernoulli mask R with R_{ij}∼Bernoulli(p)) are consistent with the dropout model described in §4 (per-case sampled Bernoulli masks) and with the linear-regression marginalization and resulting penalty derived in §9.1.

The algebraic derivation is correct: E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)w^T diag(X^TX) w, and with \tilde w=pw this yields the stated (1-p)/p factor. This matches the paper's other statements (e.g. test-time scaling W_test=pW in §4 and the interpretation in §9.1 that the regularization grows as p decreases).

The paragraph is consistent with the rest of the paper: §9.1 shows closed-form marginalization for linear regression only, the paragraph cites Wang & Manning for logistic-regression approximations, and the Conclusion (§11) states that equivalent regularizers for more complicated models (e.g., deep nets) are not obvious. Thus the paragraph’s claim that closed-form marginalization is difficult for logistic regression and deep networks and that approximations have limited applicability matches the paper’s other statements.

No other part of the paper asserts the opposite.

Table 10’s numbers (H4Z and J3V errors for Bernoulli P7V and Gaussian D4K) agree with the text in §10 that Gaussian dropout performs as well as or slightly better than Bernoulli dropout, and they do not contradict other reported results (which refer to different architectures/settings).

The retention probabilities for H4Z (hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8) agree with Appendix B.1; the J3V retention vector matches the A2F configuration cited in Appendix B.2/B.3; the D4K σ = √((1−p)/p) formula matches the derivation in §10; and the ‘‘averaging 10 random seeds’’ note aligns with Table 10. No internal contradictions were found.

The paragraph's algebra is correct and matches the paper's Section 10 treatment of Gaussian dropout: r' ~ N(1,1) = 1 + r with r ~ N(0,1), so h_i r' = h_i + h_i r (additive noise with SD |h_i|). This is consistent with the paper's variance-matching discussion (σ^2=(1−p)/p, which for p=0.5 gives σ^2=1) and with the note that mean-1 multipliers remove the need for test-time weight scaling; the implicit absolute-value of the activation for the noise SD is a minor sign nuance, not a contradiction.

No inconsistency found: the paragraph’s statements (Gaussian multiplier with mean 1 needs no test-time scaling; equivalence between scaling test weights by p and scaling training activations by 1/p; and E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p) agree with the paper’s earlier definitions and formulas (e.g. §4 W_test = p W, §9.1 the (1-p)/p term after reparameterizing with \tilde w=pw, and §10/Table 10 where σ^2=(1-p)/p).

The statement E[r_g]=1 and Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p for r_g~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p is mathematically correct and matches the paper’s earlier expressions (e.g. the Bernoulli multiplier moments and the D4K σ = √((1-p)/p) entry); no internal contradiction found.

reply.conflict: "C4Y: Code Quality" is described in the paragraph as "representing negative KL divergence between target and predicted distributions, with higher values preferred."

reply.explanation: The Appendix formula uses the background average \bar p^{s} in the log ratio (p log(q/\bar p)), which is not the negative KL divergence -D_{KL}(p||q)=sum p log(q/p). Moreover -D_{KL} is <=0, but Table 8 reports positive C4Y values; therefore the paragraph's claim that C4Y represents negative KL divergence conflicts with the paper's own formula and the reported (positive) C4Y scores.

reply.conflict: “B8T features appear coarser than the sharply defined stroke-like U2L features, with very few dead units relative to U2L;”

These two statements are inconsistent within the paper.

I found no internal contradictions: the paragraph’s claims about deterministic (marginalized) models needing no random bits and admitting gradients are consistent with the linear-regression marginalization and the discussion in §9.1–9.2 and with other parts of the paper that note marginalization is tractable in simple cases but harder for deep/logistic models.

The paragraph restates the result derived in §9.1: the marginalized objective (shown immediately after) is ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}, so features with larger scale incur larger penalty, and with ~t = p w the penalty constant is (1-p)/p (small near p→1, larger as p decreases), matching the paragraph's claims.

reply.conflict: "Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p)" (§5.2 Unsupervised Pretraining) conflicts with the setup in §4 and §9.1 that use p as the retention probability (e.g. W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} and \tilde{w}=p w).
reply.evidence: §4 (Model Description): "r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p) ..." and "W_{test}^{(l)}=p W^{(l)}." §9.1 (Linear Regression): derives the marginalized objective and then sets \tilde{w}=p w. §5.2 (Unsupervised Pretraining) states: "Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p)."
reply.explanation: If p is the probability a unit/input is retained, the expected (unthinned) input is p times the original, so to preserve pretraining outputs one should scale pretrained weights by 1/p (i.e. W_init = W_pretrain / p). Multiplying by 1/(1-p) contradicts the paper's own definition and marginalization (which imply a 1/p scaling).

reply.conflict: Paragraph 71 (and nearby sections) treats retention as a factor p on weights (writing "With \tilde{w}=p w" and using W_test = p W), implying pretrained weights should be scaled by 1/p (or that test-time weights are p times trained weights). This conflicts with §5.2, which states: "Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p), matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output."
reply.evidence: §9.1 (paragraph 71): "With \widetilde{\mathbf w}=p\mathbf w, the alternative form is ..." (shows absorbing retention as multiplication by p). §4 Model Description: "At inference, no units are removed and \mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}." §10: "... multiplying retained training activations by 1/p and leaving test weights unchanged." vs §5.2 Unsupervised Pretraining: "Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p)...".
reply.explanation: Under the paper's dropout convention (r ~ Bernoulli(p) = retention), the expected masked activation is p times the original, so to preserve pretraining outputs one should scale weights by 1/p (or equivalently treat test weights as p times training weights). The statement in §5.2 that pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p) is inconsistent with this and with the algebra in paragraph 71 and other sections.

reply.conflict: "The assumptions become successively weaker with added layers, leaving the results not directly applicable to deep networks."
reply.evidence: Same section (9.2) earlier states: "Closed-form marginalized models are difficult for logistic regression and deep nets;" (paragraph 72). Conclusion (Section 11) states: "Linear regression gives modified Y5F; equivalent regularizers for more complicated models are not obvious." Section 3 notes analytic marginalization work was "limited to models without hidden layers." These passages indicate marginalization becomes harder (i.e. requires stronger/more restrictive assumptions) as depth increases, conflicting with the claim that assumptions become "weaker" with added layers.
reply.explanation: Saying the assumptions become "weaker" with added layers contradicts the paper's repeated claim that marginalization is more difficult for logistic regression and deep (multi-layer) networks; logically, deeper networks should require stronger/more restrictive assumptions, so the word "weaker" is inconsistent with the paper's other statements.

The paragraph's claim that Gaussian multiplicative noise performs as well as or slightly better than Bernoulli dropout is supported by the paper's own results (Table 10 shows D4K slightly better than P7V on H4Z and J3V) and by the surrounding discussion in Section 10; I find no contradictory statement elsewhere in the paper.

The table’s numbers and labels (P7V = Bernoulli dropout, D4K = Gaussian dropout) agree with the Section 10 discussion and the reported experimental settings (retention p, sigma formula, architectures) elsewhere in the paper; I find no internal contradiction involving this paragraph.

The retention probabilities and averaging count match values stated elsewhere (H4Z hidden p=0.5 and input p=0.8 in Appendix B.1; J3V uses the A2F retention vector in B.2/B.3). The D4K standard-deviation formula sigma = sqrt((1-p)/p) agrees with the variance relation sigma^2 = (1-p)/p given earlier in Section 10.

The paragraph restates the equivalence derived in Section 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise): a multiplier r'~N(1,σ^2) corresponds to additive noise h_i+h_i r with r~N(0,σ^2); with σ^2=1 (e.g. p=0.5) this yields the quoted form, so there is no internal contradiction.

reply.conflict: The paragraph asserts that one can equivalently "multiply retained training activations by 1/p and leave test weights unchanged" (i.e. use a 1/p scaling for retained activations / inverted dropout), and that the Bernoulli training multiplier equals 1/p with probability p.
reply.evidence: Section 5.2 (Unsupervised Pretraining) states: "Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p), matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output."
reply.explanation: The paragraph endorses scaling by 1/p to match expected activations under dropout, but §5.2 prescribes multiplying pretrained weights by 1/(1-p) to achieve that match. For general p, 1/(1-p) ≠ 1/p (they coincide only at p=0.5), so the paper gives inconsistent prescriptions for how to scale weights/activations to match expected outputs.

The paragraph's formulas are consistent with the paper's earlier statements: the rescaled Bernoulli multiplier r_b has Var[(1-p)/p], and Table 10 gives the D4K standard deviation σ = √((1-p)/p), i.e. σ^2 = (1-p)/p, so E[r_g]=1 and Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p agree with those prior expressions.

reply.conflict: "Training takes typically 2–3 times as long as training a standard network of the same architecture."
reply.evidence: "Appendix A.2: 'High learning rate and/or momentum significantly accelerate learning.' and the practical-values table: 'QX2 learning rate relative to optimal standard-net rate | typically 10–100 times.' (Appendix A.2)." "Section 5.1: 'A proposed optimization account permits huge learning rates inside a fixed-radius weight ball...' (Section 5.1).
reply.explanation: Paragraph 79 asserts QX2 training is substantially slower (2–3×), but other parts of the paper explicitly state that QX2 permits much larger learning rates and that high learning rate/momentum 'significantly accelerate learning,' implying faster training; these statements are inconsistent within the paper.

reply.conflict: "Accelerating QX2 remains a future-work direction."

(Section 3, Related Work) and "Approximate marginalization outperforms Monte-Carlo QX2 in training time and generalization for logistic regression (Wang and Manning, 2013)." (Section 9.2, Logistic Regression and Deep Networks)

reply.conflict: 'For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units.' (and the accompanying statement 'only p n units remain in expectation') conflicts with an earlier instruction that pretrained weights be scaled by 1/(1-p).

§4 Model Description: 'r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p)' (p is the probability of retaining a unit) and 'At inference, no units are removed and W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}.'

§5.2 Unsupervised Pretraining: 'Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p), matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.'
reply.explanation: Appendix A.1 treats p as the retention probability so expected surviving units are p·(layer size) and the correct scaling to match pretraining expectations is 1/p; §5.2's use of 1/(1-p) is inconsistent with p being the retention probability and therefore contradicts the n/p expectation heuristic in Appendix A.1.

reply.conflict: The paragraph asserts that high learning rates and/or high momentum are beneficial with QX2: "High learning rate and/or momentum significantly accelerate learning... larger learning rates compensate [for QX2 noise], while higher momentum reduces the noise’s effect."

(§5.2). Appendix B.4 (N8Q) reports a concrete experiment-specific choice: "Best QX2 G6W-finetuning learning rate about 0.01," i.e. a relatively small finetuning rate rather than a very large one.
reply.explanation: Appendix A.2 presents high learning rates as a general QX2 recommendation, but the paper elsewhere explicitly recommends and uses smaller learning rates when finetuning pretrained networks (and gives an empirical small value), so the guidance is internally inconsistent without qualification.

reply.conflict: The paragraph's claim that 'QX2 learning rate relative to optimal standard-net rate | typically 10–100 times' (i.e. QX2 generally uses much larger learning rates)
reply.evidence: Section 5.2 (Unsupervised Pretraining) states: 'Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve useful pretrained information and improve final generalization relative to finetuning without QX2; rates comparable to the best randomly initialized-net rates erased that information in the initial experiments.' (§5.2). Appendix B.4 (N8Q settings) gives concrete values showing this practice: 'High learning rate | 0.1' and separately 'Best QX2 G6W-finetuning learning rate | about 0.01', indicating that for pretrained networks the paper used a smaller QX2 finetuning rate rather than a much larger one.
reply.explanation: The appendix’s blanket heuristic (QX2 uses learning rates 10–100× larger than standard) contradicts the paper's explicit advice and experimental practice for pretrained models, which recommend and employ smaller finetuning learning rates to preserve pretrained information.

reply.conflict: Appendix A.3 states a typical range for the V9C hyperparameter: "c | 3 to 4" (i.e. c between 3 and 4).
reply.evidence: Appendix B.1 (H4Z experimental settings) reports "V9C bound, all layers | c=2", meaning the paper's main H4Z experiments used c=2, which lies outside the stated typical range 3–4.
reply.explanation: The Appendix A.3 recommendation that c is typically 3–4 contradicts the concrete experimental setting in Appendix B.1 where V9C was set to c=2 for the H4Z experiments; the paper thus gives an inconsistent 'typical' range versus the value actually used in key experiments.

The paragraph is consistent with other parts of the paper: Appendix A.1 recommends a QX2 layer size of about n/p (so smaller p implies larger width), §7.3 explicitly states low retention produces underfitting while holding expected retained width helps, Appendix A.4 gives similar practical guidance on retention ranges, and the Conclusion notes stronger QX2 increases training time. reply.explanation: If the activation histogram (right plot) has a sharp zero peak—i.e. most activations are zero across cases—then the per-unit mean activations (summarized by the left histogram) should be near zero for most units; reporting "most units' mean activation" ≈ 0.7 is inconsistent with that definition and with the stated meaning of sparsity.

The paragraph's claims (underfitting at low p, error falling then rising near p=1, and that keeping pn fixed requires larger n for smaller p so inference networks differ in size) agree with Appendix A.1, B.1 and the 7.3 table/figure descriptions which state small p needs larger n (pn fixed), report errors for fixed-architecture vs fixed-expected-width (2.7% vs 1.7%), and give the flat interval 0.4≤p≤0.8 and rising error near p=1.

The retention-interval, the p choices, and the reported error figures in this paragraph are consistent with the paper's discussion of rate effects in §7.3, the fixed-expected-width experiment described in Appendix B.1, and the recommended default p≈0.5 given elsewhere (Appendix A.4). I found no internal contradiction within the paper.

The axis labels, tick ranges and curve descriptions for Figure 9 (retention p from 0.0 to 1.0; classification error axis spanning ~0–3.5%) are compatible with the paper’s reported error rates and the textual discussion of retention effects (e.g., the 0.4≤p≤0.8 flat interval and example errors of 1.7% and 2.7%). No internal contradictions were found.

reply.conflict: Paragraph 57 (§7.4) states: 'The two smallest tested training sets show no QX2 improvement.' This conflicts with the paper's earlier claim in §6: 'Generalization improved over non-QX2 neural nets on every tested data set.'
reply.evidence: §6 (Experimental Results) opening: 'Generalization improved over non-QX2 neural nets on every tested data set; ...' vs §7.4 (Paragraph 57): 'The two smallest tested training sets show no QX2 improvement: the network can memorize them despite the removal noise.'
reply.explanation: The paper asserts a universal improvement across all tested data sets in §6, but §7.4 subsequently claims that for two tested (small) training-set sizes there was no improvement; as written these two statements are mutually inconsistent.

reply.conflict: "Figure 10" horizontal-axis ticks list dataset size: 10^2, 10^3, 10^4, 10^5 (i.e. up to 100,000).
reply.evidence: Appendix B.1 (H4Z data-size comparison) states the actual 'Randomly selected data-size-comparison training sets' were 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K (maximum 50,000), so the experiments never used 100,000 examples (B.1). The Figure 10 paragraph (section 7.4) shows the 10^5 tick.

reply.conflict: “X9M matches T6R after sufficiently many samples and then performs slightly better, within one standard deviation; T6R is a fairly good approximation to the true model average.” (paragraph 59, §7.5)
reply.evidence: Section 4 (Model Description) states: "For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights." and later prescribes the test-time rule "W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}." (§4). These statements assert an exact equality between the dropout-averaged output and the scaled-weight test-time output.
reply.explanation: Paragraph 59 treats T6R as only an approximation to the true model average that X9M can slightly outperform. That conflicts with §4's explicit claim that test-time weight scaling gives the expected output under the dropout distribution (an exact equality as stated), since if T6R exactly equals the expectation then Monte-Carlo averaging (X9M) can only converge to the same result, not systematically beat it.

The paragraph’s claim that B8T is a mixture over retention vectors of U2L (RBM) models and that conditioning on a retention vector yields an ordinary U2L with the specified hidden units removed is exactly what Section 8.1 formalizes—see the definitions P(r;p), P(h,v|r;θ), the g(h_j,r_j) factor that enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0, and the resulting conditional distributions P(h|r,v) and P(v|h). This also matches the Introduction’s statement that the unit-removal construction extends to Boltzmann Machines.

reply.conflict: The paragraph defines the U2L joint distribution as P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z(θ)) exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), which identifies a as the hidden-unit biases and b as the visible-unit biases.
reply.evidence: Later in §8.1 the paper gives the conditionals P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ( b_j + ∑_i W_{ij} v_i ) and P(v_i=1 | h) = σ( a_i + ∑_j W_{ij} h_j ). These conditionals use b_j as the hidden bias and a_i as the visible bias, i.e. the opposite assignment to the joint definition above.
reply.explanation: The bias vectors a and b are named inconsistently: the joint distribution assigns a to hidden and b to visible units, but the subsequent conditional formulas swap their roles. This is an internal contradiction within §8.1.

The paragraph's definition of P(r;p) and P(h,v|r;θ), with g enforcing h_j=0 when r_j=0, matches the earlier description of B8T as a mixture of U2L models with independently retained hidden units (p as keep probability); no inconsistency with other parts of the paper was found.

reply.conflict: The paragraph gives P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) · σ(b_j + Σ_i W_{ij} v_i) and P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + Σ_j W_{ij} h_j), i.e. it uses b as the hidden-unit bias and a as the visible-unit bias.
reply.evidence: Earlier in Section 8.1 the joint distribution is written P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z) exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), which assigns 'a' to the h (hidden) bias terms and 'b' to the v (visible) bias terms. The conditionals quoted above (same paragraph) use the opposite assignment (b for hidden, a for visible).
reply.explanation: The notation for the bias vectors is inconsistent within the same section: the joint probability term a^T h + b^T v implies a are hidden biases and b are visible biases, but the conditional formulas swap these roles, a direct contradiction in the paper's own definitions.

reply.conflict: The paragraph presents the conditional P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + Σ_j W_{ij} h_j) (and earlier in §8.1 P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + Σ_i W_{ij} v_i)). These conditionals use a as the visible biases and b as the hidden biases.
reply.evidence: In §8.1 (Model Description) the joint distribution is defined as P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), which assigns a to hidden biases (a^T h) and b to visible biases (b^T v). Immediately after, the section gives P(h_j=1 | r_j,v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + Σ_i W_{ij} v_i) and P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + Σ_j W_{ij} h_j) — i.e. the roles of a and b are swapped relative to the joint-definition.

reply.conflict: Paragraph claim: "B8T features appear coarser than the sharply defined stroke-like U2L features, with very few dead units relative to U2L."
reply.evidence: Section 8.4 (Sparsity) states: "Without an additional sparsity-inducing regularizer, B8T learns much sparser representations than U2L." reply.explanation: The paragraph asserts B8T has very few dead units relative to U2L, but §8.4 explicitly says B8T is much sparser than U2L (many activations near zero), which implies more inactive (dead) units in B8T, not fewer; these statements contradict each other.

reply.conflict: "Without an additional sparsity-inducing regularizer, B8T learns much sparser representations than U2L."
reply.evidence: Section 8.3 (Features) states: "B8T features appear coarser than the sharply defined stroke-like U2L features, with very few dead units relative to U2L;" (§8.3). That wording implies B8T has fewer inactive ('dead') units than U2L (i.e. is less sparse), which directly contradicts the §8.4 claim that B8T is much sparser than U2L.
reply.explanation: §8.3 characterizes B8T as having very few dead units relative to U2L (suggesting U2L is the sparser model), while §8.4 asserts the opposite; the two statements about relative sparsity are inconsistent.

No inconsistency found: the paragraph’s claim that deterministic (noise-)marginalized models admit gradients and avoid random bits matches Section 9.1 (the linear-regression marginalization derivation), Section 9.2 (discussion of approximate marginalization for logistic/deep models), and the Conclusion (which notes noise marginalization benefits); there is no conflicting statement elsewhere in the paper.

The paragraph restates the algebra in Section 9.1: the marginalized objective is ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}, so the per-feature penalty scales with the feature magnitude (proportional to its standard deviation) and, with ṽ = p w, the regularization constant (1-p)/p is small near p≈1 and increases as p decreases.

The paragraph's notation and claim (X is N×D, w∈R^D, and input dimensions are masked by an N×D Bernoulli matrix R) matches the paper's earlier description of dropout as applying independent Bernoulli retention per input unit per training case and is consistent with the marginalized objective developed later in §9.1.

The algebra in the paragraph is correct and matches the paper’s earlier descriptions: taking expectations yields ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}, and substituting Ñw = p w gives the stated form with regularization strength (1-p)/p. This aligns with the text saying dropout gives a weighted L2 penalty that grows as p decreases.

reply.conflict: "The assumptions become successively weaker with added layers, leaving the results not directly applicable to deep networks."
reply.evidence: "Under reasonable assumptions, distributions of logistic-unit inputs and marginalized-model gradients are Gaussian with efficiently computable means and variances." (Section 9.2, same paragraph). The paragraph first asserts Gaussian approximations hold under reasonable assumptions, then states those assumptions become "weaker with added layers" yet concludes the results are "not directly applicable to deep networks."
reply.explanation: This is internally inconsistent: if the assumptions become weaker with more layers they should be easier to satisfy for deeper models (making the Gaussian/marginalization approximation more applicable), yet the sentence concludes the opposite. Likely a wording error (e.g. 'weaker' should read 'stronger').

The paragraph’s claim is supported elsewhere in the paper (Table 10 shows D4K ≤ P7V on H4Z and J3V), and Section 10 and related text describe moment-matching and equivalent training/test-time scalings—so there is no internal contradiction.

Table 10’s numbers and reported settings (architectures, retention p values) match the descriptions elsewhere (e.g. Appendix B.1–B.3) and support the text’s claim that Gaussian multiplicative noise performs as well as or slightly better than Bernoulli dropout, so no internal contradiction is found.

No inconsistencies found. The H4Z and J3V P7V retention values match the settings given in Appendix B (B.1–B.3), the D4K sigma expression equals the sigma = sqrt((1-p)/p) relation in §10, and the averaging=10 seeds matches Table 10.

The paragraph's algebra (r'~N(1,1) implies r'=1+r with r~N(0,1), so h_i r' = h_i + h_i r and the additive noise has variance h_i^2) is mathematically correct and aligns with the paper's later generalization r'~N(1,σ^2) and the moment-matching discussion; no other part of the paper contradicts this statement.

The paragraph is consistent: it correctly distinguishes the Gaussian-multiplier case (mean 1, so no test-time scaling needed) from the Bernoulli case (which uses test-time weight scaling p), and it states the standard equivalence between scaling weights at test time and using inverted (1/p) scaling at train time. The stated moments and variance (Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p) match the paper’s earlier formulas (e.g. Section 4’s W_test = pW and the σ^2=(1-p)/p relationship in Section 10).

The statement that choosing σ^2=(1-p)/p yields E[r_g]=1 and Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p matches the earlier derivation for the Bernoulli multiplier (E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p) and the surrounding discussion in Section 10; no internal contradiction is present.

The paragraph restates points made elsewhere (e.g. §5.1 on per-case sampled thinned networks and §9 on Monte‑Carlo QX2 vs. marginalized gradients) and matches the Conclusion (§11) about longer training; the claimed overfitting–training‑time tradeoff is also supported by Appendix A.4’s discussion of retention and training. No internal contradiction found.

The paragraph restates points made in §9: §9.1 derives the linear-regression (modified L2/Y5F) marginalizer, and §9.2 (and §3) note that closed-form/efficient equivalents for logistic regression and deep nets are difficult or only approximate; thus saying equivalent regularizers for more complicated models are not obvious and that accelerating QX2 remains future work is consistent with the paper.

reply.conflict: The paragraph asserts that "High learning rate and/or momentum significantly accelerate learning...larger learning rates compensate, while higher momentum reduces the noise’s effect."
reply.evidence: Section 5.2 (Unsupervised Pretraining): "Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve useful pretrained information and improve final generalization relative to finetuning without QX2; rates comparable to the best randomly initialized-net rates erased that information in the initial experiments." (§5.2). Appendix B.4 (N8Q settings) gives a numeric example: "High learning rate | 0.1" and separately "Best QX2 G6W-finetuning learning rate | about 0.01", indicating that much smaller finetuning rates were required when fine-tuning pretrained networks.
reply.explanation: The A.2 paragraph gives an unqualified recommendation for high learning rates/momentum to counteract QX2 noise, but elsewhere the paper explicitly advises using smaller learning rates when fine-tuning pretrained models (and provides a concrete example where the best finetuning rate is an order of magnitude smaller). These statements are inconsistent unless qualified; as written they conflict.

reply.conflict: The paragraph's claim that 'QX2 learning rate relative to optimal standard-net rate | typically 10–100 times' (i.e. QX2 typically uses learning rates 10–100× larger than optimal standard-net rates).
reply.evidence: Section 5.2 (Unsupervised Pretraining) states: 'Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve useful pretrained information and improve final generalization relative to finetuning without QX2; rates comparable to the best randomly initialized-net rates erased that information in the initial experiments.' Appendix B.4 (N8Q) reports 'High learning rate | 0.1' and 'Best QX2 G6W-finetuning learning rate | about 0.01' and notes 'The smaller learning rate was important for best results.'
reply.explanation: The Appendix's blanket guideline that QX2 typically uses much larger learning rates conflicts with the paper's explicit guidance and experimental settings showing that when finetuning pretrained networks with QX2 one should use smaller learning rates (and that smaller finetuning rates produced the best results).

reply.conflict: The paragraph’s table states the V9C hyperparameter c has a "Typical range" of 3 to 4.
reply.evidence: Appendix B.1 (H4Z experimental settings) explicitly lists "V9C bound, all layers | c=2" (i.e. the H4Z experiments used c=2). Other experiment descriptions (Appendix B.2 A2F and B.4 N8Q) list c=4, showing the paper uses values both below and inside the claimed "3 to 4" typical range.
reply.explanation: The appendix claims a typical V9C range of 3–4, but the paper’s own H4Z experimental settings use c=2, which contradicts that stated typical range. (At minimum this is an inconsistency between the recommended "typical" values and the concrete value used in a main experiment.)

The paragraph agrees with other parts of the paper: Appendix A.1/A.4 recommend sizing a QX2 layer ≈n/p (so smaller p requires larger width), Section 7.3 explicitly reports underfitting at low retention and the benefit of fixing expected retained width, and multiple sections (e.g. A.4, experiments) state input retention depends on input type and is typically closer to 1. No internal contradiction found.

The paragraph's guidance (hidden-unit p≈0.5–0.8, default near 0.5, input units nearer 1) matches other statements and experimental settings in the paper (e.g. §3 noise table, §4 discussion of defaults, and Appendices B.1/B.2/B.4 where hidden p=0.5 and input p=0.8 are used).

The paragraph’s description of holding out validation images, selecting hyperparameters by validation at a fixed training endpoint, then combining validation with training for a final run matches the detailed settings in Appendix B.1 (e.g. 10,000 held-out validation images and a 1,000,000 weight-update endpoint) and does not contradict other statements in the paper.

I found no contradictions: the hyperparameters and counts in this paragraph (e.g. held-out 10,000 validation images, 1,000,000 weight-update endpoint, hidden p=0.5/input p=0.8, depths {2,3,4} × widths {1024,2048} = 6 architectures, largest two-layer model >65M parameters, architectures used for regularizer- and data-size comparisons) agree with the settings and results described elsewhere (Tables, §6.1.1 and Appendix B.1).

I found no internal contradiction: the paragraph’s claims about two- vs three-layer H4Z results match Table 2 and the B.1 discussion of the large 2- and 3-layer experiments; the fixed-expected-width statement matches §7.3 and Appendix A.1; and the description of X9M agrees with §7.5 and B.1.

The statements about the A2F training-count being approximate, the split into standard and extra labeled portions (with validation drawn from both), and the choice to normalize RGB pixels (with GCN/ZCA tried but not helpful) are consistent with the detailed settings given later in Appendix B.2 and with other dataset-specific preprocessing descriptions; no internal contradiction was found.

I found no internal inconsistencies between this paragraph and other parts of the paper: the validation counts, architecture (3 conv + 2 fc), per-layer retention vector (6 values for input+3 conv+2 fc), V9C and momentum values all match the paper’s other descriptions and tables.

reply.conflict: The paragraph states: "Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images" (for J3V and W6R).
reply.evidence: Table 1 (Data-set overview) earlier in the paper lists the J3V/W6R row as: "J3V/W6R | Vision | 3072 (32 × 32 color) | 60K | 10K", i.e. 60K training images.
reply.explanation: The paragraph's claim that each of J3V and W6R has 50,000 training images contradicts Table 1, which reports 60,000 training images for J3V/W6R.

The paragraph describes dataset-specific preprocessing for J3V/W6R and does not assert anything that contradicts other statements in the paper; other sections (e.g. A2F) describe different preprocessing choices for different datasets, so there is no internal inconsistency.

The paragraph's details (Kaldi log-filter-bank features, monophone alignments, 21-frame windows, mean-centered unit-variance inputs) agree with other parts of the paper (Table 1 gives 2520 = 120×21 dimensionality; Appendix B.4 settings list 21 frames and mean-centering/unit-variance). No other statement in the paper contradicts the speaker count or the described recording conditions.

The listed N8Q settings (21-frame window; input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5; V9C c=4; momentum 0.95; high learning rate 0.1 with G6W finetune ≈0.01; G6W pretraining = RBMs trained with CD-1) align with the dataset summary (Table 1), the Appendix A heuristics for retention, momentum and V9C, and the §6.2 / Appendix B.4 descriptions of the N8Q experiments—no contradictory statements appear elsewhere in the paper.

No internal contradiction detected. The statement that V9C gave no improvement for G6W finetuning is a dataset-specific observation compatible with the paper’s earlier claim that V9C usually helps (not always), and the M5X counts/Dimensionality (402,738 articles, 2,000-word vocabulary, resulting in slightly more than 200,000 examples per split) are consistent with Table 1’s rounded 200K/200K training/test entries.

The paragraph’s statements (3665 exons = 2932 train + 733 test, 1014 features, four tissue types, and three states {inc, exc, nc} per tissue) agree with Table 1, the C4Y formula in Appendix B.6 (summing over tissue types and states), and the Section 6.4 description of three splicing-related states, so no internal conflict is present.

reply.conflict: The paragraph defines C4Y as C4Y = sum_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^{s} log( q_t^{s}(r_i) / \bar p^{s} ) (i.e. dividing by the global average \bar p^{s}), which conflicts with the paper's earlier claim that C4Y "represent[s] negative KL divergence between target and predicted distributions."
reply.evidence: Section 6.4 (Z7P discussion) states: "scored by a distributional measure (C4Y: Code Quality) representing negative KL divergence between target and predicted distributions, with higher values preferred." Appendix B.6 / the paragraph in question (where \bar p^{s} is defined as the average of p_{i,t}^{s} over i,t) gives the formula C4Y = sum_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^{s} log( q_t^{s}(r_i) / \bar p^{s} ).
reply.explanation: Negative KL divergence -KL(P||Q) would be sum_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^{s} log(q_t^{s}(r_i)/p_{i,t}^{s}); replacing the per-example target p_{i,t}^{s} by the global average \bar p^{s} yields a different quantity, so the formula contradicts the earlier description of C4Y as negative KL divergence.

I found no internal inconsistency: the paragraph’s architecture and hyperparameters (two layers of 1024 units, hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7, V9C, 5-fold averaging) agree with the experimental details for Z7P in Appendix B.6 and with the paper’s earlier statements that QX2 uses thousands of hidden units while the Bayesian model uses only a few tens (and with the reported results in Table 8).

reply.conflict: The header claims the article appears in "Journal of Machine Learning Research 15 (2014) 1929–1958".
reply.evidence: The paper's internal "Original-page map" (immediately below the header) enumerates pages beginning at 1930 and ending at 1955 (e.g., '1930—Figure 1 and Introduction' ... '1955—B.3 continuation and B.4–B.6'), which conflicts with the 1929–1958 range in the header.
reply.explanation: The page range given in the header (1929–1958) is inconsistent with the internal page map (1930–1955), so the paragraph's stated journal pagination does not match the paper's own page listing.

reply.conflict: "Original-page map, including continuations: 1930—Figure 1 and Introduction; ... 1955—B.3 continuation and B.4–B.6." (i.e. the paragraph’s page map covering pp. 1930–1955)
reply.evidence: "Journal of Machine Learning Research 15 (2014) 1929–1958" (paper header at the top of the document), which states the article spans pages 1929–1958

reply.conflict: '...computational-biology experiments attain state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks.' (Abstract claim that QX2 achieves SOTA on computational-biology)
reply.evidence: Section 6.4 and Table 8 (Z7P results) conflict with that claim: Table 8 lists 'Neural Network with QX2' = 567 and 'Bayesian Neural Network (Xiong et al., 2011)' = 623 for C4Y (bits), and Section 6.4 explicitly states this metric uses 'higher values preferred.' Thus Table 8 shows the Bayesian network scores better than QX2 on Z7P. Additionally, Section 7.4 states 'The two smallest tested training sets show no QX2 improvement: the network can memorize them despite the removal noise,' which contradicts the abstract's sweeping claim of improvements across domains.
reply.explanation: The abstract asserts QX2 attains state-of-the-art in computational-biology, but the paper's own Table 8 (and the stated preference that higher C4Y is better) shows a Bayesian neural network outperforming QX2 on Z7P; moreover Section 7.4 admits QX2 yields no improvement on the smallest datasets, contradicting the abstract's broad claim of consistent benchmark gains.

reply.conflict: The paragraph's claim that the proposed construction "approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions."
reply.evidence: Elsewhere the paper describes the ensemble quantity being approximated as the (Monte‑Carlo) average of sampled members' predictions and compares methods to that sample average: Introduction (earlier/later lines) states a more expensive alternative "X9M: Monte‑Carlo model averaging" "averages sampled members’ predictions"; §7.5 says "X9M matches T6R after sufficiently many samples... T6R is a fairly good approximation to the true model average" and discusses the finite‑sample average’s approach to the true average; §11 (Conclusion) says "A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates their averaged predictions." These passages treat the target as an (arithmetic) model average, not a geometric mean.
reply.explanation: The paragraph asserts approximation to a geometric mean, but elsewhere the paper consistently frames the target ensemble as the (Monte‑Carlo) averaged predictions and evaluates T6R against that average; geometric vs arithmetic averaging are different, so the wording in the paragraph is inconsistent with the rest of the paper.

The paragraph’s points—that sampling noise can induce spurious training relationships and that standard remedies include early stopping, soft weight sharing and weight penalties (L1/L2)—are consistent with the rest of the paper, which repeatedly discusses overfitting, early stopping, L1/L2 (Y5F/O3U), other regularizers (V9C), and dropout as an alternative/augmentation (e.g., §§1,5,9 and the regularization experiments).

reply.conflict: The paragraph asserts that 'separately training many large nets makes output averaging prohibitively expensive' and that 'Even successful training of many such models leaves their joint inference infeasible for rapid-response applications.'
reply.evidence: Section 6.1.4 (Table 6, ILSVRC-2012 validation/test results) reports 'Avg of 5 Conv Nets + QX2 (Krizhevsky et al., 2012)' and gives improved Top-1/Top-5 errors, i.e. the paper presents and evaluates an ensemble of five separately trained large convolutional nets. Section 7.5 ('X9M vs. T6R') and Figure 11 discuss Monte-Carlo model averaging (X9M), noting that X9M matches the weight-scaling approximation after about k=50 samples and can perform slightly better—treating averaging multiple predictions as a practical, evaluated option.
reply.explanation: The paragraph claims that training and jointly inferring many large networks is prohibitively expensive and infeasible at test time, but elsewhere the paper both reports results from averaging several separately trained large ConvNets and analyzes Monte-Carlo averaging as a feasible procedure; this contradicts the paragraph's blanket infeasibility claim.

reply.conflict: The paragraph's claim that 'the former gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularization methods across varied classification problems.'
reply.evidence: Section 7.4 (Data-Set Size) states: 'The two smallest tested training sets show no QX2 improvement: the network can memorize them despite the removal noise.' (This directly contradicts the implication of broadly lower generalization error.) Additionally, Section 6 earlier claims 'Generalization improved over non-QX2 neural nets on every tested data set,' which conflicts with Section 7.4's admission of exceptions.
reply.explanation: The paragraph asserts broad/general superiority of T6R/QX2 across varied problems, but elsewhere the paper explicitly reports datasets where QX2 provides no improvement; the paper therefore contains inconsistent statements about the universality of QX2's generalization benefit.

The caption and paper map accurately reflect content elsewhere: §2–§9 and Appendix A appear with the described topics, and the depiction of a thinned network (units removed with their connections) matches the formal model in §4 and related figures.

The paragraph gives an evolutionary analogy (sexual recombination breaking co-adaptations and yet prevailing), which is reiterated and extended later (the Livnat et al. account) to motivate dropout breaking co-adaptations. No other statement in the paper contradicts this description.

The paragraph's account (randomly selected partners discourage co-adaptation and favor independently useful features; replication is a poor robustness strategy) matches other statements in the paper (e.g. §2 Motivation's sexual-recombination analogy and §7.1 'Breaking co-adaptations is proposed as the principal source...') and the experimental results; I find no internal contradiction.

The paragraph is a metaphor illustrating why breaking large, fragile co-adaptations is beneficial; this matches other statements (e.g., Section 2’s discussion of sexual recombination and Section 7.1’s claim that dropout breaks co-adaptations to improve generalization) and does not contradict any other part of the paper.

The paragraph is consistent with the rest of the paper: Section 4 defines T6R (weight scaling) and the Related Work table earlier in §3 reports S2H typical noise ≈5% versus QX2 input ≈20% and hidden ≈50%, supporting the claim that T6R/dropout can use much higher noise than typical DAEs.

The reported noise levels (S2H ~5%, QX2 input removal ~20%, QX2 hidden removal ~50%) agree with other statements in the paper (e.g., Appendix A.4: input retention typically 0.8, hidden-unit typical range 0.5–0.8; §7.3 and experimental tables use p=0.5 and p=0.8). The remark that the adversarial-removal models have no hidden units is consistent with the paper's other mentions of these prior works, so no internal contradiction is found.

The paragraph's claims about analytic marginalization yielding deterministic regularizers in simple cases and the cited scope of related work (van der Maaten et al., Chen et al., Wang and Manning) are consistent with the paper's later discussion in §9 (including §9.1 and §9.2), which presents linear-regression marginalization and notes difficulties extending closed-form marginalization to deeper models.

reply.conflict: The paragraph asserts: "For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights."
reply.evidence: Section 9.2 ("Logistic Regression and Deep Networks") states: "Closed-form marginalized models are difficult for logistic regression and deep nets; under reasonable assumptions, distributions of logistic-unit inputs and marginalized-model gradients are Gaussian ... leaving the results not directly applicable to deep networks." By contrast, Section 9.1 shows the equality only in the linear case: "QX2 linear regression is, in expectation, ridge regression..." reply.conflict: The paragraph first defines the layer index as "l ∈ {1,...,L} index them" (i.e. l starts at 1 for hidden layers) but immediately afterwards uses "For l ∈ {0,...,L-1} ..." when giving the feed-forward equations (i.e. l including 0).

reply.conflict: The section (§4) asserts that "for every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights" while the paragraph explicitly allows arbitrary non-linear activations (e.g. the logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x))).

reply.explanation: Exact equality E[output_under_dropout] = output_with_scaled-weights requires linearity (E[f(z)] = f(E[z]) only for linear f). The paper simultaneously claims the equality for "every hidden unit" while permitting non-linear activations and elsewhere acknowledges that marginalization/weight-scaling is exact only in simple (linear) cases and otherwise an approximation, so the universal equality claim is inconsistent with those later statements.

The paragraph restates the model equations ({r_j^{(l)}} Bernoulli, {~widetilde{y}^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}}) and matches later descriptions (e.g. §5.1 on per-case sampled subnetworks and Appendix B reporting input retention values). No internal contradiction is found.

The paragraph’s description of Figure 3 (gates r producing masked outputs \widetilde y and otherwise unchanged operations) matches the formal definition in §4 (r_j ~ Bernoulli(p), \widetilde{\mathbf y}^{(l)}=\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)}, and z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}), so there is no internal conflict.

reply.conflict: The paragraph's claims that 'QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and the incoming-weight constraint (V9C) gives a further significant boost' and that 'that constraint usually improves deep-net stochastic-gradient training even without QX2.'

reply.conflict: "Stochastic gradient descent differs from standard-net training only in its per-case sampled thinned network" (Paragraph 22).

reply.explanation: The parameter names a and b are used inconsistently: the energy/partition expression assigns a to hidden biases and b to visible biases, but the conditional-probability formulas in this paragraph swap those roles, a clear notational contradiction within the paper.

reply.conflict: The paragraph asserts P(v_i=1 | \mathbf h) = \sigma\big(a_i + \sum_j W_{ij} h_j\big).
reply.evidence: Section 8.1 (Model Description) defines the joint U2L distribution as P(\mathbf h,\mathbf v;\theta) = (1/Z) exp(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h + \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h + \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v), which assigns \mathbf a as the hidden-unit biases and \mathbf b as the visible-unit biases. In the same section the hidden conditional is written P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\big(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i\big), which (again) uses b_j where the joint form indicates the hidden bias should be a_j. These equations show that the conditionals in Section 8.1 swap a and b relative to the joint definition.
reply.explanation: The paper uses a and b inconsistently: the joint distribution indicates a is the hidden bias and b the visible bias, so the visible conditional should be \sigma(b_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j) and the hidden conditional should use a_j. The paragraph's visible-conditional formula conflicts with the earlier parameter naming (and the hidden-conditional formula also reflects the swap).

The paragraph’s claims (B8T features are coarser than U2L and B8T has very few dead units relative to U2L) do not contradict other statements: Section 8.4 reports B8T yields much sparser representations (and Figures 12/13 illustrate the compared feature and activation patterns). The paper does not elsewhere assert the opposite for B8T, so no internal inconsistency is found.

reply.conflict: 'Without an additional sparsity-inducing regularizer, B8T learns much sparser representations than U2L.' (Section 8.4) — i.e. B8T is claimed to be much sparser than U2L.
reply.evidence: Section 8.3 (Features) states: 'B8T features appear coarser than the sharply defined stroke-like U2L features, with very few dead units relative to U2L;' (Section 8.3). Also Section 7.2 defines sparsity as requiring low average activity per unit across cases, so 'sparser' should imply more units with low/near-zero average activity (i.e. more dead or near-dead units).
reply.explanation: Section 8.4 asserts B8T is much sparser than U2L, but Section 8.3 explicitly says B8T has very few dead units relative to U2L; given the paper's own definition of sparsity (few active units per case and low average activity per unit), these two statements are contradictory.

The paragraph's claim that deterministic (noise-)marginalized models need no random bits and admit gradients is supported by Section 9.1 (closed-form marginalization for linear regression) and Section 9.2 (approximate marginalization for logistic regression/deep nets) and is explicitly contrasted elsewhere with Monte-Carlo sampling (X9M); no other part of the paper asserts the opposite.

The paragraph matches the derivation given later in §9.1: the marginalized objective becomes ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}, so dimensions with larger input variance incur larger penalties, and with ṽw = p w the regularization constant is (1-p)/p, which is small when p≈1 and grows as p decreases.

The paragraph’s use of an N×D Bernoulli mask R (R_{ij}∼Bernoulli(p)) and the stated marginalized objective agree with the paper’s earlier description of per-example independent Bernoulli dropout on inputs and with the later derivation that dropout yields an L2-like regularizer for linear regression; no internal contradiction is found.

The algebra in the paragraph is correct and agrees with the paper’s other statements: it shows marginalized dropout for linear regression equals a ridge-like penalty p(1-p) diag(X^T X), and with \tilde w=pw this becomes (1-p)/p times the same per-dimension penalty. This matches the paper’s earlier informal descriptions (penalty grows as p decreases, and marginalization yields an L2-type regularizer) and the definitions used elsewhere, so there is no internal inconsistency.

reply.conflict: "The assumptions become successively weaker with added layers, leaving the results not directly applicable to deep networks."
reply.evidence: Section 9.2 (paragraph 72) immediately states both that "distributions of logistic-unit inputs and marginalized-model gradients are Gaussian with efficiently computable means and variances" under reasonable assumptions and then asserts "The assumptions become successively weaker with added layers, leaving the results not directly applicable to deep networks." (Section 9.2, para 72). These two clauses are in direct adjacency in the same paragraph.
reply.explanation: The paragraph claims the assumptions become weaker with more layers (which would make the Gaussian approximation easier to satisfy and thus more applicable), yet immediately concludes the results are not directly applicable to deep networks; the two claims contradict each other.

The paragraph's assertion that multiplicative Gaussian noise performs as well as or slightly better than Bernoulli dropout is supported elsewhere in the paper (see Table 10, which shows D4K slightly outperforming P7V on H4Z and J3V), and Section 10 also derives the matched moments (E=1, Var=(1-p)/p) used to justify the comparison. No internal contradictions were found.

Table 10’s reported errors and experiment settings agree with the descriptions in Section 10 and the experimental details in Appendix B (architectures, retention probabilities and averaging over seeds); I find no internal contradiction with other results in the paper.

The retention values and σ formula in paragraph 75 match the settings given in Table 10 and the descriptions in §10 and Appendices B.1–B.3 (e.g. H4Z hidden p=0.5/input p=0.8, J3V retention tuple, and σ^2=(1−p)/p), so there is no internal contradiction.

The paragraph's algebra (r'=1+r with r~N(0,1) so h_i r' = h_i + h_i r and the noise std = |h_i| when Var(r)=1) matches the paper's earlier derivation that a Gaussian multiplier N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p matches the Bernoulli multiplier's mean and variance (for p=0.5 giving σ^2=1). Any sign/absolute-value phrasing is a notational detail, not a contradiction.

No internal contradiction found: the paragraph’s statements about Gaussian multipliers (mean 1 removing the need for test-time weight scaling), the inverted-dropout view with r_b taking value 1/p w.p. p (so E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p), and matching σ^2=(1-p)/p are consistent with the paper’s earlier formulas (Section 4’s W_test = p W, Section 10’s table and discussion, and Section 9.1’s (1-p)/p term).

The stated choice sigma^2=(1-p)/p implies E[r_g]=1 and Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p, which matches the paper's earlier derivation that the (inverted) Bernoulli multiplier has Var=(1-p)/p and the Table 10/D4K specification sigma = sqrt((1-p)/p); there is no internal contradiction.

The paragraph is consistent with the rest of the paper: Section 5.1 describes per-case sampled thinned networks and stochastic per-case gradients, Section 9 contrasts Monte‑Carlo QX2 (stochastic gradients) with deterministic marginalization (which admits true marginalized gradients), and the paper elsewhere (end of §11 and Appendix A.2) notes extra gradient noise, higher learning‑rate/momentum tuning and that accelerating QX2 is future work — all supporting the claim of longer (≈2–3×) training and that computed gradients are not gradients of the final inference network.

reply.conflict: "Accelerating QX2 remains a future-work direction."
reply.evidence: Section 9.2 (Marginalizing QX2) states: "Approximate marginalization outperforms Monte-Carlo QX2 in training time and generalization for logistic regression (Wang and Manning, 2013)." Section 9 earlier also cites Srivastava (2013) and Wager et al. (2013) discussing marginalization and QX2 as a regularizer.
reply.explanation: The concluding sentence claims acceleration of QX2 is future work, but Section 9.2 explicitly reports prior work (Wang and Manning, 2013) that already accelerates QX2 for logistic regression and discusses deterministic marginalization techniques, so the paragraph is inconsistent with those earlier statements.

The recommendation to use ≈n/p units so that the expected number of active units is n is consistent with other parts of the paper (e.g. §7.3 and Appendix B.1 discuss holding expected retained width pn constant and note that smaller p requires larger n). No other statement in the paper contradicts this heuristic.

The paragraph’s claims match other parts of the paper (e.g. §5.1 and §11 describe QX2’s added gradient noise and recommend high momentum and large decaying learning rates; Appendix A.2 and experiment settings (B.4, B.1) give concrete high learning-rate and high-momentum recommendations). No internal contradiction was found.

reply.conflict: 'QX2 learning rate relative to optimal standard-net rate | typically 10–100 times' (i.e. the paragraph's claim that QX2 typically uses much larger learning rates than standard nets).
reply.evidence: Section 5.2 (Unsupervised Pretraining) states: 'Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve useful pretrained information and improve final generalization relative to finetuning without QX2; rates comparable to the best randomly initialized-net rates erased that information in the initial experiments.' (§5.2). Appendix B.4 (N8Q settings) gives concrete numbers: 'High learning rate | 0.1' and 'Best QX2 G6W-finetuning learning rate | about 0.01', showing a QX2 finetuning rate smaller than the stated high rate (Appendix B.4).
reply.explanation: The appendix asserts QX2 typically requires much larger learning rates, but earlier the paper explicitly recommends smaller finetuning learning rates when using QX2 after unsupervised pretraining and provides an experiment where the best QX2 finetuning rate (0.01) is lower than the 'high' rate (0.1), which contradicts the blanket 10–100× larger-rate recommendation.

reply.conflict: The paragraph states the V9C hyperparameter c has a "typical range" of 3 to 4.

reply.conflict: 'Input-unit optimum in general | closer to 1 than to 0.5' (from Appendix A.4)

The paragraph's procedure (10,000 held-out validation images; hyperparameters chosen by validation at the fixed endpoint; then validation+training combined and a final run to the same endpoint) matches the detailed settings in Appendix B.1 (e.g. “Held-out training images for validation | 10,000” and “Weight-update endpoint … | 1 million”) and the described H4Z procedure elsewhere (B.3), so no internal inconsistency is found.

I found no internal contradictions: the validation size, update endpoint, architecture sweep, retention probabilities, momentum, V9C bound, architecture choices and the various experiment-specific settings in this paragraph are consistent with the tables, figures and descriptions elsewhere in the paper (e.g., Tables 2 and 9, Section 7.3, Appendix A and the rest of Appendix B).

The paragraph restates results already reported elsewhere: B.1/Table 2 show very wide two-layer nets outperform three-layer counterparts at the same QX2 settings; §7.3 and Appendix A.1 describe the fixed-expected-width notion (pn) and that small p implies larger n; and §7.5/B.1 state that X9M (Monte‑Carlo averaging) approaches the true model average as k→∞. These points are consistent with the paper's other statements.

The paragraph’s values (validation split summing to 600 per class → 6000 total, three conv layers + two FC layers, retention vector of six values mapping to input+3 conv+2 FC, V9C c=4, momentum=0.95) match the paper’s descriptions elsewhere (A.2 recommendations, §6.1.2 results and Table 10/J3V comparisons) and do not contradict other reported numbers or statements.

reply.conflict: "Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images..." (B.3)
reply.evidence: Table 1 (Data-set overview, §6) lists J3V/W6R with Training set = 60K and Test set = 10K (Table 1), which contradicts the 50,000 training-image claim in B.3.

The paragraph’s statements about applying per-channel global contrast normalization and ZCA whitening for J3V/W6R, and that architecture and retention rates match the A2F configuration, do not contradict other parts of the paper (Appendix B.2 lists A2F preprocessing and retention; Table 10 and B.2/B.3 show the same retention settings). No internal inconsistency is found.

The paragraph’s claims (680 speakers × 10 sentences, Kaldi log-filter-bank features, monophone forced alignment, 21-frame windows predicting the central frame, and mean-centered/unit-variance inputs) are consistent with the paper’s N8Q descriptions elsewhere (Table 1: 2520 = 120-dim × 21 frames; Appendix B.4: 'Consecutive frames per window | 21' and mean-centering/unit-variance inputs and Kaldi feature/label pipeline). No internal contradiction is found.

The paragraph’s settings (21-frame window; input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5; momentum 0.95; a high training LR of 0.1 with a smaller finetuning LR ≈0.01; decay schedule; G6W pretraining with CD-1) are consistent with other parts of the paper (Table 1 lists 21 frames for N8Q; §3/Table of typical noise levels and Appendix A.4 recommend input≈0.8 and hidden≈0.5; §5.2 recommends smaller finetuning rates for pretrained nets), so there is no internal contradiction.

reply.conflict: "equal-sized training and test splits result in more than 200,000 training examples."
reply.evidence: "Table 1 (Section 6, Data-set overview) lists M5X with Training set 200K and Test set 200K; Appendix B.5 states the used subset contains 402,738 articles (so an equal split would yield ~201,369 per split)."
reply.explanation: Table 1 reports 200K training and 200K test for M5X, while Appendix B.5 gives a total of 402,738 articles whose equal split implies ≈201,369 examples per split (i.e. >200,000). The two statements differ (Table 1 appears to round to 200K).

The paragraph’s counts and structure (3665 exons = 2932+733 from Table 1, 1014 features, four tissue types, and three states per tissue: inc/exc/nc) agree with the dataset summary in Table 1 and the C4Y formula and earlier text that sum over tissue types and the three splicing states.

reply.conflict: The paragraph gives C4Y = \sum_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^{s} \log\left(\frac{q_t^{s}(r_i)}{\bar p^{s}}\right), but Section 6.4 describes C4Y as "representing negative KL divergence between target and predicted distributions". Negative KL would be \sum_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^{s} \log\left(\frac{q_t^{s}(r_i)}{p_{i,t}^{s}}\right), whereas the formula uses \bar p^{s} (the dataset average) rather than p_{i,t}^{s}, so it is not the negative KL between the per-example target and predicted distributions.
reply.evidence: Section 6.4: "scored by a distributional measure (C4Y: Code Quality) representing negative KL divergence between target and predicted distributions, with higher values preferred." (§6.4). Appendix B.6 / paragraph 98 gives the formula C4Y = \sum_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^{s} log(q_t^{s}(r_i)/\bar p^{s}) and defines \bar p^{s} as the average of p_{i,t}^{s} over i,t. Table 8 (in §6.4) lists C4Y scores (440, 463, 487, 567, 623), which are large positive numbers; if C4Y were the negative KL (i.e. -D_{KL}), values should be <= 0.
reply.explanation: The textual description (negative KL) and the explicit formula conflict: the formula uses the global average \bar p^{s} in the denominator instead of the per-example target p_{i,t}^{s}, so it does not compute negative KL. Moreover, calling the measure "negative KL" is inconsistent with the positive C4Y values reported in Table 8, since negative KL (−D_{KL}) cannot exceed zero.

The paragraph’s settings (QX2 scale ~1000s, Bayesian nets a few tens, trained QX2 = two layers of 1024 units, hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7, V9C, 5-fold averaging) match the descriptions given for Z7P in Appendix B.6 and Section 6.4; I found no other statements in the paper that contradict these specific parameter/architecture choices.
The title, author list, and submission/publication information in this paragraph match the rest of the paper; no conflicting statements were found elsewhere.

reply.conflict: The paragraph's "Original-page map" enumerates pages 1930 through 1955 (e.g. "1930—Figure 1 ... 1955—B.3 continuation and B.4–B.6."), implying the article's page coverage is 1930–1955.
